Twenty Third Indian Antarctic Expedition
Ministry of Earth Sciences, Technical Publication No. 21, pp 127-136
Retrieval of in-situ Lake Bottom Sediment Cores  
from Schirmacher Oasis: A prelude to palaeoclimatic  
studies using lacustrine sedimentation in Antarctic
environment
D. Jayapaul, Rajesh Asthana and S. Jayaram
Geological Survey of India
ABSTRACT
Climatic changes have a significant effect on the glacial and periglacial regions 
adjacent to the large inland ice masses of Antarctica. A perspective on climatic 
variability can be obtained by the study of sedimentation within the lacustrine 
systems.
An attempt was made during the expedition to retrieve long, in-situ lake 
bottom sediment cores using an indigenously designed and fabricated sediment 
coring system developed by the authors at Antarctica Division, GSI, considering 
the field constraints and extreme antarctic climate.
INTRODUCTION
Schirmacher Oasis is situated in the peripheral region of central 
Dronning Maud Land, East Antarctica between 70°44’ 33" S -  70o46'30" S 
latitudes and 11 °22f 04" E -  11 °54’ 00" E longitudes. The low lying hills of the 
oasis are bounded in south by the polar ice cap, ice-shelf lies to the north 
and entire area is interspersed with more than a hundred fresh water lakes 
(Fig. 1). The size of these lakes varies from a few hectares to a few km2  and 
the maximum depth of water in them ranges from a few meters to about 
150m. Depending upon their disposition, lakes in Schirmacher Oasis have 
been classified as proglacial, landlocked or inland and epishelf lakes 
(Ravindra et a l, 2002). Majority of these lakes occupy ice-scoured basins 
and troughs(Fig.2) vacated by retreating glaciers, though some lakes follow 
well defined lineaments and show elements of structural control (Beg et al., 
2006).
Modem glacial environments hold an essential key to our knowledge 
of present processes of erosion, transport and deposition, particularly within

the lacustrine environment that furnishes evidence as to how these processes 
operate. The H uttonian principle (“present is key to the past”) of 
understanding the present to permit a grasp of the past and of the future 
becomes very pertinent in understanding the dynamic processes of modem

glacial environments. Lacustrine system of Schirmacher Oasis holds a rich 
repository of information within the sedimentary layers at the lake bottom. 
The uninterrupted nature of sedimentation in lacustrine environments can 
be used to reconstruct the past climate spanning historical to geological 
time scales based on their sedimentological characteristics -  including 
provenance, transport mechanisms, interacting tectonics, if any, drainage 
and biological content. High resolution palaeoclimatic data can be obtained 
from sediment cores using sedimentological, elemental geochemistry, diatoms, 
plants and animal microfossils, lithology and mineral magnetic properties.
PALEO CLIM ATIC STUDIES: LAKE BO TTOM  SEDIM ENT  
CORES
In-situ  lake bottom sediment cores are most significant tool in the 
palaeoclimatic studies. Indian endeavor of lake sediment coring was initiated 
during 16th  Indian Antarctic expedition using Hydro-Bios gravity corer. 
Sediment samples including short cores of about 45 to 60 cm were collected 
from two lakes of Schirmacher Oasis. Sedimentological and mineralogical 
characteristics of the lacustrine sediments from Schirmacher were dealt by 
Sinha & Chatterjee (2000).
Palynological investigations of various polar surface deposits and lake 
sediment cores from Schirmacher Oasis have generated'quite useful pollen 
data on the past polar climatic events and episodes. At present, understanding 
of many aspects remains poor. Three folds climatic oscillations (arid-warm, 
humid warm and more humid) are recorded from one meter long polar lake 
sediments from Zub and long lakes during late Holocene (8,000 years BP) 
as evidenced by the fluctuation of the values of long distance transported 
micro biota along with local moss spores and algal assemblages ( Bera, 
2004). A nother 50 cm long sedim ent core from Zub Lake yielded 
thecamoebians (Mathur et al., 2006). Although more detailed study is required 
but it is possible to elucidate the past climatic oscillation in polar region 
through palynostratigraphy (Bera and Khandelwal, 2003; Bera, 2006) using 
well corroborated pollen diagram and pollen-spore deposition model.
